source: Dış kaynaklarda saptanan eksik soru tipleri; bağımsız anlatım ve resmî cevap kontrolü (2026-10-13)
answer_convention: İki dilde aynı sırada; ilk şık doğru. Belirsiz cevap aktif bankada yok.
id_convention: Kalıcı idler_040.json; eski veya emekli kimlik yeniden kullanılmaz.

questions.text: In daylight, a pilot looks into featureless haze for a long time without identifying a distant object to focus on. The eyes relax and focus at a relatively short distance, so distant traffic becomes harder to detect. What is this condition called?
options: Empty-field myopia
Autokinesis
A false-horizon illusion
Astigmatism

questions.text: Why can even a small amount of alcohol add to a pilot’s impairment when cabin pressure altitude increases?
options: Its depressant action makes the brain more susceptible to hypoxia
Falling cabin pressure necessarily raises blood alcohol concentration for the same alcohol dose
The oxygen percentage in inhaled air decreases as cabin pressure altitude increases
At altitude, alcohol mainly acts as a stimulant and increases the brain’s oxygen demand

questions.text: At low level in a strong steady wind, an aircraft makes a coordinated turn from downwind to into-wind while maintaining indicated airspeed. What pair of impressions can the ground cues create?
options: An outward skid and an apparent decrease in airspeed
An outward skid and an apparent increase in airspeed
An inward slip and an apparent decrease in airspeed
An inward slip and an apparent increase in airspeed

questions.text: A vivid recent accident report comes easily to mind and dominates a pilot’s risk estimate, while representative frequency data are neglected. Which bias is illustrated?
options: Availability bias
A guarantee that vivid reports are statistically representative
A physical change of the aircraft’s stall speed
Correct calculation of risk from every available observation equally

questions.text: Why can a very early start during the pilot’s biological night impair alertness even if the flight itself is short?
options: The circadian phase can favour sleep and low alertness independently of flight duration
A short flight automatically cancels all circadian effects
The body clock is always locked to UTC for every pilot
The aircraft’s latitude directly eliminates sleep need

questions.text: In an aeroplane with a cabin heater using an exhaust heat exchanger, a suspected leak is accompanied by headache and dizziness. Which response addresses possible CO exposure?
options: Apply the AFM response: shut off the suspected heater source, admit fresh air and use available supplemental oxygen while arranging a safe landing and medical help
Increase cabin heat to remove the gas
Continue because CO must always have a noticeable smell
Wait for cherry-red lips before taking any action

questions.text: After many flights using one routine, a pilot is given a different instruction but unintentionally starts the old familiar sequence. What has happened?
options: Habit capture: a learned routine has overridden the current intended action
A deliberate decision to violate a rule in every case
Proof that the new instruction must have been wrong
A guarantee that automatic routines cannot make errors

questions.text: An inadvertent night thunderstorm encounter exposes the pilot to lightning flashes. Which cockpit-lighting adjustment in FAA weather guidance helps reduce temporary flash blindness?
options: Increase cockpit illumination to reduce the contrast with the lightning flashes
Make the cockpit as dark as possible to maximise the contrast
Stare directly at every flash
Use a dark tint that prevents instrument reading

questions.text: When choosing cockpit sunglasses, which combination protects vision without unnecessarily distorting colour-coded information?
options: Effective UV protection and a suitable neutral tint with adequate visible-light transmission
The darkest possible tint regardless of instrument readability
A strong blue-blocking tint that makes navigation-light colours indistinguishable
Any dark lens, because darkness alone guarantees UV protection

questions.text: For optimum protection, FAA AIM medical guidance encourages supplemental oxygen above approximately which cabin pressure altitudes in (1) daytime and (2) nighttime flight?
options: Neither until loss of consciousness occurs

questions.text: According to FAA AIM recommended waiting times for actual flight altitudes up to 8,000 ft AMSL, what minimum pair applies after a compressed-air dive (1) without decompression stops and (2) requiring decompression stops?
options: (1) 12 hours; (2) 24 hours
(1) 4 hours; (2) 12 hours
(1) 24 hours; (2) 12 hours
(1) no waiting; (2) 4 hours

questions.text: A correctly calibrated three-pointer altimeter has no instrument fault. Can a pilot still read the wrong altitude because of display interpretation?
options: Yes; indication accuracy and human readability are different, so the needles can still be misinterpreted
No; correct calibration makes the pointer arrangement unambiguous to every pilot
No; three pointers automatically prevent thousand-foot reading mistakes
Yes; any reading mistake proves that the static-pressure system was faulty

questions.text: In a simple optical model, an eye with hyperopia would focus parallel rays behind the retina. Which spectacle lens moves the focus toward the retina?
options: A converging lens with positive power, commonly described as convex
A diverging lens with negative power, commonly described as concave
A neutral filter with zero optical power only
An opaque lens that admits no light

questions.text: Can both successful and unsuccessful past experiences influence a pilot’s decisions in a new flight situation?
options: Yes; past experience can influence assessment and choice, while current conditions must still be evaluated
Only successful experiences can influence decisions
Only unsuccessful experiences can influence decisions
No; previous experience is unrelated to any new aviation decision

questions.text: Which acceleration condition is associated with a visual red-out?
options: Negative vertical g, forcing blood toward the head.
Positive vertical g, drawing blood away from the head.
Steady1g level flight with a normally supplied brain.
A loss of cabin pressure without any change in acceleration.

questions.text: A pilot is breathing rapidly and has tingling fingers, but a fingertip pulse oximeter shows a normal oxygen-saturation value. What is the valid conclusion?
options: A normal reading does not exclude hyperventilation and is not a complete fitness assessment.
A normal reading proves that hyperventilation is impossible.
The instrument directly measures the carbon-dioxide level in the blood.
The reading proves that symptoms can safely be ignored.

questions.text: Which blood component plays a central role in forming a plug to stop bleeding after a vessel is injured?
options: Platelets (thrombocytes).
Red blood cells carrying oxygen.
The dissolved nitrogen content.
Haemoglobin acting as an immune cell.

questions.text: A pilot reads a pointer-and-scale instrument from an oblique angle rather than directly in front of it. What reading error can this cause?
options: Parallax error.
Compass acceleration error.
Altimeter temperature error.
Gyroscope drift caused by Earth rotation.

questions.text: A laser illuminates the cockpit during a night approach. Which effect makes this an immediate flight-safety concern?
options: Dazzle, distraction and temporary visual impairment can compromise control and orientation.
It guarantees immediate permanent total blindness in every case.
It changes the magnetic heading of the compass.
It improves night adaptation by increasing retinal sensitivity.

questions.text: Why are polarised sunglasses generally not recommended in a cockpit containing LCD displays or polarising windscreen materials?
options: Their interaction with those materials can obscure displays or create misleading visual patterns.
They always remove all useful light regardless of lens orientation.
They cause carbon-monoxide poisoning.
They make the eye unable to change focus permanently.

questions.text: Which two dimensions are combined in a basic aviation risk-assessment matrix?
options: Likelihood of the event and severity of its consequences.
Pilot experience and the cost of insurance only.
Aircraft colour and remaining daylight.
The number of passengers and their willingness to fly only.

questions.text: A pilot favours reports supporting the planned route and dismisses credible reports contradicting it. What cognitive bias does this illustrate?
options: Confirmation bias.
An unbiased cross-check of independent evidence.
A positive exchange of flight controls.
Correct readback of an ATC clearance.

questions.text: An aircraft remains controllable but is unintentionally flown into terrain. Which term describes this accident category?
options: Controlled Flight Into Terrain (CFIT).
Loss of Control In Flight (LOC-I).
A deliberate precautionary landing.
A runway incursion before takeoff.

questions.text: After identifying a flight hazard, which set contains recognised ways to deal with its risk?
options: Eliminate or avoid it, mitigate it, transfer suitable elements, or consciously accept it.
Ignore it, conceal it, postpone all evaluation, or assume it cannot occur.
Transfer all PIC responsibility to passengers or to ATC.
Treat every hazard as equally acceptable without considering consequences.

questions.text: A pilot proposes an unnecessary low pass mainly to impress friends. Which hazardous attitude is most directly illustrated?
options: Macho: taking risks to prove ability.
Resignation: believing personal action cannot influence the outcome.
A disciplined application of personal minima.
An appropriate response to an immediate distress situation.

questions.text: An autopilot has worked reliably for many flights, so the pilot stops monitoring its modes and flight path. What human-factor risk is increasing?
options: Complacency and loss of awareness of automation behaviour.
Guaranteed improvement in situational awareness.
Removal of the need to be ready for manual flight.
Elimination of the possibility of incorrect mode selection.

questions.text: Why is using alcohol to help fall asleep a poor strategy before flying?
options: It can reduce restorative sleep quality even if it makes falling asleep seem easier
It guarantees more restorative sleep in every person
It permanently removes circadian disruption
It compensates for all sleep debt without affecting flight performance

questions.text: A high cabin-altitude warning occurs after loss of pressurisation at high altitude, and a suitable oxygen mask is available. What immediate personal-protection priority comes before diagnosing the fault?
options: Don the oxygen mask and establish oxygen flow while maintaining aircraft control
Complete a lengthy diagnosis before using oxygen
Wait for impaired judgement to prove that oxygen is required
Remove the mask to make radio calls clearer

questions.text: Hyperventilation is known to be the problem, aircraft control is maintained, and hypoxia or CO exposure has been excluded. Which breathing response helps?
options: Consciously reduce the excessive rate and depth toward normal breathing
Breathe faster and deeper to remove still more carbon dioxide
Hold the breath repeatedly until fainting
Use a paper bag as an automatic first response to any unexplained flight symptom

questions.text: A pilot recalls the particular place, time and personal experience of their first solo flight. Which long-term-memory category is being used?
options: Episodic memory of a specific event
Semantic memory of a general fact alone
Procedural memory of how to move a control alone
A sensory trace that can exist only during the original visual stimulus

questions.text: Can coffee or a cold shower rapidly remove alcohol from the body and establish fitness to fly?
options: No; they do not accelerate alcohol elimination or establish safe performance
Yes; either immediately returns blood alcohol to zero
Yes; caffeine guarantees immunity to alcohol-related hypoxia
Yes; feeling alert proves that alcohol and hangover effects are absent

questions.text: A cataract is a cloudy area in which eye structure?
options: The lens
The cornea solely because of astigmatism
The optic-nerve exit solely because of the normal blind spot
The iris solely because of colour-deficient cones

questions.text: While following one conversation, a pilot’s attention is suddenly drawn to their own call sign in another conversation. Which phenomenon is illustrated?
options: Attentional breakthrough from meaningful information, commonly called the cocktail-party effect
Perfect conscious processing of every simultaneous message
A hearing loss caused by middle-ear pressure
A guarantee that divided attention has unlimited capacity

questions.text: Which outside visual information can help a pilot estimate height and closure near the runway during the round-out?
options: Ground or runway texture, perspective and the apparent motion of nearby terrain
Radio loudness alone as an exact height measurement
Only the colour of the runway lights, independent of perspective
The number of passengers, independent of the visible scene

questions.text: At night, a runway is visible but the unlit approach area has few ground features. What dangerous height illusion can a “black hole” approach create?
options: The aircraft may seem too high, encouraging an unduly low approach
The aircraft necessarily seems too low, so every pilot climbs
It guarantees an accurate natural horizon
It causes only colour blindness and cannot affect the approach path

questions.text: During an approach, rain on the windscreen creates an illusion that the aircraft is higher than it really is. What approach error can follow?
options: Flying a lower approach than intended
Flying a higher approach because the aircraft seems too low
A guaranteed increase in true altitude with no control change
Only a radio-frequency error

questions.text: Which distinction between acute and chronic fatigue is useful for flight fitness?
options: Acute fatigue is short-term; chronic fatigue involves prolonged or accumulated impairment that may require more than one normal rest period
Acute fatigue lasts for years, while chronic fatigue lasts only seconds
Chronic fatigue always vanishes after drinking coffee
Experience makes both kinds harmless

questions.text: During a non-urgent joint decision, how can a pilot leading the discussion reduce the influence of rank on the other person’s input?
options: Invite independent observations and suggestions before announcing a preferred answer
Announce the answer first and accept only agreement
Forbid questions because leadership excludes disagreement
Delegate all responsibility and refuse to make any decision

questions.text: A checklist is interrupted by a radio call. On resuming it, what helps prevent an omitted item?
options: Re-establish the last positively completed item and resume using the published checklist procedure
Guess where the sequence was and continue from memory
Mark all remaining items complete because most are routine
Restart an unrelated familiar checklist

questions.text: A pilot and instructor combine independent observations to find a safer solution than either identified alone. What team effect does this illustrate?
options: Synergy: effective cooperation adds benefit beyond separate individual contributions
Proof that any two people always make a safer decision
A transfer of all PIC responsibility to the instructor
A physiological increase in oxygen percentage

questions.text: A cockpit alert must attract the pilot’s attention. What further property is essential?
options: It must clearly identify the condition and convey the appropriate urgency without unnecessary confusion
It should be as startling as possible even if its meaning cannot be identified
It should suppress all other flight information indefinitely
It should use the same indistinguishable signal for every condition

questions.text: A pilot acknowledges that conditions have become unsuitable but feels obliged to finish the original trip because much time and effort have already been invested. What decision trap is illustrated?
options: Plan-continuation bias or press-on-itis
An independent reassessment that automatically validates the old plan
A requirement imposed by having filed a flight plan
A rule that diversion is only permitted before take-off

questions.text: With congested nasal passages, a descent produces severe pain over an eyebrow or upper cheek. Which pressure mechanism can cause this?
options: Failure to equalise trapped air in a sinus with increasing cabin pressure
Nitrogen bubbles caused by a rapid ascent only
Loss of hearing from noise damage to the cochlea
A necessary increase in oxygen percentage during descent

questions.text: What does it mean for an aviation system to be tolerant of a human error?
options: An error can occur without its consequences seriously jeopardising safety
The system guarantees that people can never make an error
Only experienced pilots may make errors without consequences
Every latent error is permanently hidden from detection

questions.text: In very cold conditions a pilot is shivering and the body’s oxygen demand is increased. How can this affect susceptibility to hypoxia?
options: It can make the same limited oxygen supply less adequate for the increased demand
It always increases the atmospheric oxygen percentage
It guarantees immunity to altitude hypoxia
It makes every oxygen system unnecessary

questions.text: In the standard three-stage skill-acquisition model, what is the usual progression as a novice practises a flight task?
options: Cognitive → associative → automatic or autonomous
Automatic → cognitive → associative
Associative → automatic → cognitive
Cognitive → automatic → associative

questions.text: Altitude-induced decompression sickness is suspected in flight. The symptoms lessen during a safe descent. What is the appropriate response?
options: Continue the appropriate oxygen/emergency response, land as soon as possible and obtain urgent medical evaluation
Continue the planned flight because reduced symptoms prove complete recovery
Climb again to verify whether the pain returns
Exercise the painful joint vigorously to remove the bubbles

questions.text: During a cockpit discussion one person says nothing but displays a hesitant expression and posture. What should be understood about communication?
options: Non-verbal behaviour can convey meaning even without spoken words
Silence always proves agreement and understanding
Communication is impossible unless both people speak simultaneously
Body language replaces the need for any explicit safety statement

questions.text: A learner repeats important verbal information and links it to existing knowledge to help retain it beyond working memory. What process is this?
options: Rehearsal supporting encoding into longer-term memory
Chunking that guarantees unlimited working-memory capacity
A vestibular reflex that stores the information permanently
Sensory adaptation to brighter light

questions.text: Which route correctly describes normal blood flow through the ventricles?
options: Right ventricle: oxygen-poor blood to the lungs; left ventricle: oxygen-rich blood to the body
Right ventricle: oxygen-rich blood to the body; left ventricle: oxygen-poor blood to the lungs
Both ventricles send oxygen-rich blood only to the lungs
Both ventricles receive blood from the body and pump it directly to the brain

questions.text: After agreeing with one another, two pilots accept a riskier plan than the average of their initial individual preferences. What group effect is this?
options: Risky shift, the high-risk side of group polarisation
A guarantee that all group decisions are always riskier
A physiological reduction in hearing
A rule that the senior pilot is no longer responsible

questions.text: A person has a reduced amount of functioning haemoglobin due to anaemia. How can this increase susceptibility to hypoxia?
options: It reduces the blood’s oxygen-carrying capacity despite oxygen being available to breathe
It increases the percentage of oxygen in the atmosphere
It always prevents nitrogen from dissolving in tissues
It makes the lungs produce additional oxygen

questions.text: In altitude-induced decompression sickness, which organ system is affected by the manifestation called “the chokes”?
options: The lungs and respiratory system
Only the finger joints
Only the retina
Only the outer ear canal

questions.text: Several hours after a high-altitude exposure, a pilot develops possible decompression-sickness symptoms although the flight has ended. Is being at ground level sufficient reassurance?
options: No; delayed DCS can occur after return to ground level and requires prompt medical assessment
Yes; DCS cannot exist once the aircraft has landed
Yes; ordinary exercise always removes the cause
No; the pilot must immediately make another high-altitude flight

questions.text: In typical age-related hearing loss, which sounds are commonly affected first?
options: Higher-frequency sounds
Only the very lowest frequencies
Every frequency necessarily disappears at the same instant
Only sounds travelling through the middle ear bones

questions.text: Why can photochromic sunglasses work less effectively in a cockpit than outdoors?
options: Their darkening depends on UV exposure, which windscreens can reduce, and their clearing may be too slow for rapid light changes
They always eliminate the need for clear lenses at night
They darken instantly solely from cockpit air pressure
They correct every pilot’s refractive error without a prescription

questions.text: What is the basic function of retinal photoreceptors after light reaches the retina?
options: Convert light into signals that can be carried through the visual nervous system to the brain
Refract most incoming light before it enters the pupil
Regulate cabin pressure
Generate oxygen for the optic nerve

questions.text: For a nearby object, what does binocular stereopsis use to help judge depth?
options: Slightly different images from the two eyes
The sound level measured in decibels
The middle-ear pressure difference
Only the colour of the distant horizon

questions.text: Why can gradually developing pilot incapacitation be especially dangerous?
options: The impairment may remain unrecognised while the pilot continues making degraded decisions
It always produces an immediate, unmistakable collapse
It automatically improves judgement before recovery
It is harmless if the pilot has many flight hours

questions.text: During descent, ear pressure cannot equalise and pain increases. Safe level flight or a small climb is available with the required clearance. Which action avoids continuing to increase the pressure difference?
options: Pause the descent and allow equalisation; use the safe authorised altitude adjustment if appropriate
Increase the descent rate to build outside pressure faster
Keep descending rapidly because hearing loss proves equalisation
Remove supplemental oxygen to reduce middle-ear pressure

questions.text: What normally contributes to a pilot’s mental model of the current flight situation?
options: Both past knowledge or experience and current sensory information
Only past experience, regardless of current evidence
Only an automatic motor routine, with no current information
A perfect recording of all sensory inputs without interpretation

questions.text: A pilot faces a genuinely unfamiliar problem for which no learned rule fits. Which performance mode is mainly needed to work out a solution?
options: Knowledge-based reasoning using understanding of the situation and system
Automatic skill-based execution of an unrelated familiar routine
Rule-based application of a rule known to be unsuitable
A deliberate violation as the only possible way to solve any novel problem

questions.text: A pilot stares at one isolated light against a dark background and the stationary light seems to move. What illusion is this?
options: Autokinesis
A false horizon caused by a sloping cloud bank
Coriolis illusion caused by moving the head during a sustained turn
A normal change of the light’s true bearing proving collision

questions.text: Sound intensity level is expressed in decibels. What kind of scale is the decibel scale?
options: Logarithmic
Linear, so doubling the number always doubles sound intensity
A direct measure of frequency in hertz
A measure of hearing duration in seconds

questions.text: Before a training flight with another pilot, what should an effective operational briefing establish?
options: A shared understanding of the plan, responsibilities and responses to likely problems
Only that the senior person must never be questioned
Only social conversation to improve the atmosphere
Every possible detail without checking whether it was understood

questions.text: What does a sensory detection threshold describe?
options: The minimum stimulus strength needed to elicit a sensory response under the stated conditions
The maximum amount of information retained permanently
The total number of checklist items memorised
A guarantee that every physically detected signal becomes consciously noticed

questions.text: What does hypoglycaemia mean, and why can it impair a pilot?
options: Abnormally low blood glucose, which can cause weakness, confusion and reduced performance
Low oxygen partial pressure with a normal blood glucose level
High blood glucose that always improves concentration
An increase of carbon dioxide caused solely by a blocked ear

questions.text: Which autonomic division generally supports recovery and “rest and digest” functions after a stress response?
options: Parasympathetic division
Sympathetic division responsible for fight or flight
Voluntary skeletal-muscle system only
The visual cortex alone

questions.text: A pilot has several continuing worries and a demanding flight ahead. How should their combined stress be assessed?
options: The demands can accumulate and together exceed the pilot’s ability to cope
Each demand cancels out the others
Only the most recent worry has any effect
Experience guarantees immunity to all combined stress

questions.text: A pilot is becoming rushed and overloaded before departure. Which response addresses avoidable causes of the stress?
options: Allow preparation time, reconsider the plan and reduce unnecessary demands before committing
Keep the same plan and hide symptoms with alcohol
Rush through checks so less time is available to worry
Assume cockpit stress disappears as soon as the aircraft becomes airborne

questions.text: Before selected information reaches working memory, which store briefly holds incoming visual and auditory impressions?
options: Sensory memory, including visual iconic and auditory echoic traces
Semantic long-term memory only
Procedural memory containing learned motor skills
The permanent storage of all stimuli without any selection

questions.text: After much practice, a familiar control sequence can be performed smoothly with little conscious attention. What best describes this learned sequence?
options: A motor programme or learned automatic routine
An unlearned innate reflex that never required practice
A knowledge-based solution to an entirely novel problem
Proof that checklists and monitoring can always be abandoned

questions.text: A task exceeds a pilot’s knowledge and skill even though there is enough time to do it. Which workload problem is this?
options: Qualitative overload: the task is too difficult for the available capability
Quantitative overload caused solely by too many simple tasks in too little time
Underload caused by a lack of stimulation
A guarantee of optimal performance because ample time is available

questions.text: A pilot correctly intends to set a particular radio frequency but accidentally enters a different digit. Which kind of error is this?
options: A slip: the intended plan is correct but the action is not carried out as intended
A mistake: the pilot deliberately planned the wrong action
An intentional violation of a known rule
A physiological loss of consciousness

questions.text: A pilot uses an acronym to remember a sequence of safety checks. What memory aid is being used?
options: A mnemonic linking information to a memorable pattern
A new physiological sense
An increase in the physical size of working memory
A method guaranteeing that every recalled item is correct without verification

questions.text: The AFM identifies time-critical emergency memory items. After completing those immediate actions while controlling the aircraft, what should the pilot do?
options: Use the applicable checklist to verify and complete the remaining procedure
Perform every remaining item from memory even when a checklist is available
Start an unrelated checklist solely because it is familiar
Assume the emergency is solved and omit all further checks

questions.text: According to FAA aeromedical guidance, approximately what cabin pressure altitude can already begin to impair night vision in an otherwise healthy pilot?
options: About 5,000 ft.
Only above 18,000 ft.
Only above 35,000 ft.
No altitude can affect night vision while oxygen remains21% of air.

questions.text: During daytime VFR flight, which lookout method helps detect traffic across the windscreen?
options: Scan systematically in small sectors, pausing briefly to focus in each.
Sweep the eyes continuously as fast as possible without pausing.
Keep looking at one fixed point and rely entirely on peripheral motion.
Watch only the area directly ahead of the nose.

questions.text: A pilot holds a valid medical certificate but develops an illness that could impair the flight. Who must make the immediate decision not to exercise the licence privileges?
options: The pilot, with aeromedical advice as appropriate.
Only the examiner who issued the certificate.
ATC, after the aircraft departs.
The passengers, by a majority vote.

questions.text: In a positive transfer of flight controls, pilot A says “You have the flight controls” and pilot B replies “I have the flight controls”. What completes the recommended three-step exchange?
options: Pilot A confirms “You have the flight controls” and verifies the transfer.
Pilot B repeats “You have the flight controls”, returning control immediately.
Both pilots release the controls simultaneously.
No further confirmation is needed once the first statement is made.

questions.text: A pilot notices the thought “rules do not apply to me today”. What is the first step in correcting this hazardous attitude?
options: Recognise and label the thought as hazardous before applying its antidote.
Immediately act on it to prevent hesitation.
Suppress all checklists to reduce workload.
Wait for an accident to prove that the thought was hazardous.

questions.text: A pilot displays impulsivity and thinks “I must do something immediately”. Which corrective attitude is appropriate?
options: Pause and think before acting
Rules do not apply to me
Nothing I do can help
Accidents only happen to others

questions.text: A pilot displays anti-authority and thinks “Nobody should tell me what to do”. Which corrective attitude is appropriate?
options: Respect and follow the applicable rules
Act before thinking
Assume an accident cannot happen to me
Give up because the outcome is fate

questions.text: A pilot displays invulnerability and thinks “An accident cannot happen to me”. Which corrective attitude is appropriate?
options: Accept that it could happen to me and manage the risk
Prove superior skill by taking the risk
Do the first thing that comes to mind
Assume rules apply only to other pilots

questions.text: What does presbycusis mean in a pilot’s hearing assessment?
options: Gradual hearing loss associated with ageing.
Temporary ear-pressure pain during descent.
Vertigo caused by head movement during a turn.
Conductive blockage caused solely by an object in the outer ear.

questions.text: A distant aircraft is approaching directly on a collision course at a high closing speed. How does its apparent size usually change as impact approaches?
options: It grows slowly at first, then very rapidly near impact.
It grows at a constant rate throughout the approach.
It grows rapidly at first, then its apparent size becomes constant.
Its apparent size remains unchanged until the aircraft pass.

questions.text: In daylight VMC with a clearly visible, reliable natural horizon, which reference normally gives the best direct information about aircraft attitude?
options: The real external horizon.
The sensation of balance in the inner ear.
Pressure felt through the seat alone.
The apparent slope of a nearby cloud surface.

questions.text: Two pilots are exposed to cockpit noise at different sound levels and for different lengths of time. What must be considered when assessing the risk of noise-induced hearing damage?
options: Both the sound level and the duration of exposure.
Only the loudest instantaneous sound level.
Only the duration, regardless of sound level.
Only whether the sound contains speech.

questions.text: Sunlight repeatedly flickers through a rotating propeller and a passenger feels disoriented. Which action directly reduces this visual stimulus while the pilot maintains safe control?
options: Shield the passenger from the flickering light, for example with a suitable visor or shade.
Make the flicker brighter to speed adaptation.
Ask the passenger to stare steadily through the propeller.
Increase the cabin temperature to remove the visual effect.

questions.text: A pilot starts using a non-prescription antihistamine. Does its over-the-counter status establish that it is safe to use before flying?
options: No; the illness and medicine must both be assessed, with aeromedical advice when needed.
Yes; only prescription medicines can impair flying.
Yes, provided the first dose was taken less than an hour ago.
No; every medicine permanently invalidates the pilot licence.

questions.text: A pilot accustomed to hazy conditions flies into unusually clear air. What distance-perception error can occur?
options: Distant terrain may seem nearer than it really is.
Distant terrain must seem farther away than it really is.
The actual distance to terrain is reduced by clearer air.
The terrain position becomes independent of visual contrast.

questions.text: Friends are waiting for a leisure flight, but the crosswind exceeds the pilot’s personal limit and conditions are worsening. What is the sound decision?
options: Postpone the flight despite the passengers’ disappointment.
Let the passengers decide whether the risk is acceptable.
Depart promptly so that the planned schedule is preserved.
Use the flight to practise exceeding personal limits.

questions.text: During a flight with a more experienced pilot, you notice an action that appears immediately unsafe. What is the appropriate communication response?
options: Promptly and clearly state the safety concern.
Remain silent because experience guarantees correctness.
Wait until landing regardless of the urgency.
Express agreement now and discuss the concern only with someone else later.

questions.text: An instrument is intended to show whether a value is increasing rapidly or approaching a limit. Which presentation often makes that trend easiest to recognise at a glance?
options: A well-designed analogue scale or graphical trend indication.
A numerical value with no scale or trend context.
A warning that appears only after the limit is exceeded.
A display that changes units automatically without notice.

questions.text: Before a normal training flight you cannot find the correct aircraft checklist. What should you do?
options: Obtain the correct checklist before proceeding with the planned checks.
Use a checklist for another type with similar controls.
Omit the checks because an instructor will be aboard.
Rely on memory for every check to avoid delaying departure.

questions.text: A long flight in a hot cockpit increases a pilot’s water loss. Which consequence is a concern as dehydration develops?
options: Fatigue and reduced mental and physical performance.
An automatic increase in tolerance to hypoxia.
Improved concentration because less fluid is circulating.
Protection from heat illness even without drinking.

questions.text: A passenger feels airsick during a manoeuvring flight. Which measure may reduce the discomfort without administering medication?
options: Reduce unnecessary manoeuvring, provide fresh air and encourage looking at a stable outside reference.
Increase abrupt manoeuvres so the passenger adapts faster.
Ask the passenger to make repeated rapid head movements.
Have the passenger focus only on a close moving object inside the cabin.

questions.text: A piston aeroplane has a small exhaust leak into the cabin. Why can the resulting carbon-monoxide exposure be more hazardous at a higher cabin altitude?
options: Reduced oxygen availability adds to the loss of oxygen-carrying capacity caused by CO.
Higher altitude makes CO turn into harmless nitrogen.
CO has less affinity for haemoglobin at lower cabin pressure.
Higher altitude guarantees the pilot can smell CO sooner.

questions.text: Can a pilot reliably exclude carbon monoxide in the cabin merely because no unusual smell or colour is noticed?
options: No; carbon monoxide itself is colourless and odourless.
Yes; dangerous CO always has a sharp smell.
Yes; CO always produces a visible grey cloud.
Yes; CO becomes noticeable to the senses before it affects performance.
